question.prompt:
Suppose \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are positive integers such that \[\frac{a}{14} + \frac{b}{15} = \frac{c}{210}.\] Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

I. If \(\gcd(a, 14) = 1\) or \(\gcd(b, 15) = 1\) or both, then \(\gcd(c, 210) = 1.\)

II. If \(\gcd(c, 210) = 1,\) then \(\gcd(a, 14) = 1\) or \(\gcd(b, 15) = 1\) or both.

III. \(\gcd(c, 210) = 1\) if and only if \(\gcd(a, 14) = \gcd(b, 15) = 1.\)

solutions.title: Test each prime divisor
solutions.explanation:
Only the primes \(2,3,5,7\) can give \(c\) a common factor with \(210\), so testing these four primes will determine when the gcd is \(1\).

Multiplying the equation by \(210\) gives
\[
c=15a+14b,
\qquad 210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7.
\]
We reduce this equation modulo each prime. The notation \(x\equiv y\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(x-y\).

For \(2\), we have \(c\equiv a\pmod2\). Thus \(2\) divides \(c\) exactly when \(2\) divides \(a\).

For \(3\), we have \(c\equiv2b\pmod3\). Thus \(3\) divides \(c\) exactly when \(3\) divides \(b\).

For \(5\), we have \(c\equiv4b\pmod5\). Thus \(5\) divides \(c\) exactly when \(5\) divides \(b\).

For \(7\), we have \(c\equiv a\pmod7\). Thus \(7\) divides \(c\) exactly when \(7\) divides \(a\).

For the tests involving \(3\) and \(5\), multiplying by \(2\) cannot supply a factor of \(3\), and multiplying by \(4\) cannot supply a factor of \(5\). This explains why those multipliers do not change the divisibility tests.

Thus \(c\) avoids all four primes exactly when \(a\) avoids \(2\) and \(7\), and \(b\) avoids \(3\) and \(5\). Equivalently,
\[
\gcd(c,210)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gcd(a,14)=\gcd(b,15)=1.
\]
This proves III. It also proves II, because having both gcds equal to \(1\) guarantees that at least one is \(1\).

For I, take \(a=1\) and \(b=3\). Then \(c=15+42=57\). Although \(\gcd(a,14)=1\), we have \(\gcd(57,210)=3\), so I is false.

Therefore, \(\boxed{\text{II and III only}}\) are necessarily true, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

solutions.title: Relate the gcds directly
solutions.explanation:
Adding or subtracting a multiple of a number does not change common divisors with that number. Applying this fact to \(14\) and \(15\) gives direct relationships between the three gcds.

Clearing denominators yields
\[
c=15a+14b=a+14(a+b)=15(a+b)-b.
\]
If a positive integer divides \(14\), then it divides \(c\) exactly when it divides \(a\), because \(c-a\) is a multiple of \(14\). Similarly, any divisor of \(15\) divides \(c\) exactly when it divides \(b\), because \(c+b\) is a multiple of \(15\). Therefore,
\[
\gcd(c,14)=\gcd(a,14),
\qquad
\gcd(c,15)=\gcd(b,15).
\]
The numbers \(14\) and \(15\) have no common prime factor. Consequently, the prime factors common to \(c\) and \(210=14\cdot15\) split between these two gcds, giving
\[
\gcd(c,210)
=\gcd(c,14)\gcd(c,15)
=\gcd(a,14)\gcd(b,15).
\]
Both factors on the right are positive integers. Their product equals \(1\) if and only if both equal \(1\). This proves III and, in particular, II.

Statement I requires only one factor on the right to equal \(1\), which is insufficient. For a concrete counterexample, choose \(a=2\), \(b=1\), and hence \(c=44\). Then \(\gcd(b,15)=1\), but \(\gcd(c,210)=2\).

Thus the necessarily true statements are \(\boxed{\text{II and III only}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
